newsitem.title: UK: London and Manchester says H1 business up.
newsitem.headline: London and Manchester says H1 business up.

text.p: British life and corporate pensions firm London and Manchester Group Plc said on Monday new annual premium business for the first half of 1997 had increased in all of its divisions, with an overall group rise of 16 percent over the same period in 1996.
London and Manchester's chairman David Hubbard welcomed the Labour government's review of retirement provision.

But its intention to phase out a 20 percent tax credit on dividends to pension funds "will undoubtedly have a negative impact on either the long term cost of pensions provision or on the level of benefits accruing to scheme members and personal pension holders," he said.

Hubbard said employers' efforts to provide quality corporate pension schemes to their employees had been undermined and it was "time to reverse this unwise trend and to give fresh encouragement to employers to start and maintain high quality occupational schemes".

London and Manchester's annual premiums rose to 14.8 million stg for the period, up from 12.8 million stg for the first six months in 1996. But single premium products dropped to 23.8 million stg from 26.6 million and managed fund investments fell to 27.5 from 28.1 million stg.

The group said its new industrial branch business was up by over 90 percent, new ordinary branch business was up by 19 percent in home service and by five percent in the appointed representatives network.
It said its corporate pensions division business was up by 11 percent, including a 16 percent increase in pensions business.
"These results demonsatrate progress right across the group," Hubbard said.
A major contribution had, he said, come from London and Manchester's subsidiary estate agency operation where new annual premiums were up by 30 percent as a result of a strong housing market.

Hubbard said meeting recently set deadlines by the Personal Investment Authority (PIA) for compensating customers wrongly advised to opt out of occupational schemes and take out personal pensions remained the group's top priority.
